claim: Odor responses in olfactory bulb degrade under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia.
source: In recordings from head-fixed mice, we found that odor responses in olfactory bulb degrade under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia while responses immediately downstream, in piriform cortex, remain robust.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings in head-fixed mice comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: Odor responses in piriform cortex remain robust under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia.
source: In recordings from head-fixed mice, we found that odor responses in olfactory bulb degrade under ketamine/xylazine anesthesia while responses immediately downstream, in piriform cortex, remain robust.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings in head-fixed mice comparing awake and anesthetized states.

claim: Recurrent connections are required to stabilize cortical odor representations across states.
source: Recurrent connections are required to stabilize cortical odor representations across states.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental manipulations of recurrent circuitry using TeLC and comparisons between semilunar and pyramidal cells.

claim: Piriform odor representations exhibit attractor dynamics within and across trials.
source: Moreover, piriform odor representations exhibit attractor dynamics, both within and across trials, and these are also abolished when recurrent circuitry is eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing pattern stabilization and persistence of odor representations.

claim: Attractor dynamics in piriform cortex are abolished when recurrent circuitry is eliminated.
source: Moreover, piriform odor representations exhibit attractor dynamics, both within and across trials, and these are also abolished when recurrent circuitry is eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using TeLC to eliminate recurrent connections.

claim: Recurrently-connected piriform populations stabilize sensory representations in response to degraded inputs.
source: Here, we present converging evidence that recurrently-connected piriform populations stabilize sensory representations in response to degraded inputs, consistent with an auto-associative function for piriform cortex supported by recurrent circuitry.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including cross-state decoding and cell-type specific manipulations.

claim: Pattern completion requires being able to reliably identify a familiar object even when the stimulus is noisy or degraded.
source: Recognition occurs at the interface of perception and memory: it requires being able to reliably identify a familiar object, even when the stimulus is noisy or degraded, or when behavioral states change.
evidence: This claim draws from established understanding of pattern completion in cognitive neuroscience.

claim: Recurrent neural networks can perform pattern completion through auto-associative recall.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that this retrieval can occur in recurrent neural networks through processes called auto-associative recall, attractor dynamics, or pattern completion (Hopfield, 1982; Marr, 1971; Haberly and Bower, 1989; Hasselmo et al., 1990; Treves and Rolls, 1994; Eichenbaum, 2004; Rolls, 2013; Guzman et al., 2016; Chaudhuri and Fiete, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies on recurrent neural networks.

claim: Pattern completion has been observed in hippocampus.
source: Phenomenological evidence for pattern completion has been described in various recurrent networks, including hippocampus (Nakazawa et al., 2002; Wills et al., 2005; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014), piriform cortex (Chapuis and Wilson, 2012), and neocortex (Suzuki and Gottlieb, 2013; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016; Inagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in hippocampus.

claim: Pattern completion has been observed in piriform cortex.
source: Phenomenological evidence for pattern completion has been described in various recurrent networks, including hippocampus (Nakazawa et al., 2002; Wills et al., 2005; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014), piriform cortex (Chapuis and Wilson, 2012), and neocortex (Suzuki and Gottlieb, 2013; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016; Inagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in piriform cortex.

claim: Pattern completion has been observed in neocortex.
source: Phenomenological evidence for pattern completion has been described in various recurrent networks, including hippocampus (Nakazawa et al., 2002; Wills et al., 2005; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014), piriform cortex (Chapuis and Wilson, 2012), and neocortex (Suzuki and Gottlieb, 2013; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016; Inagaki et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in neocortex.

claim: Whether pattern completion requires recurrent connectivity has not been demonstrated.
source: However, despite recurrent collateral connections being a defining feature of auto-associative networks, whether these phenomena indeed require recurrent connectivity has not been demonstrated.
evidence: This claim is based on a gap in the existing literature identified by the authors.

claim: Odors are initially encoded as combinations of co-active glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
source: Odors are initially encoded as combinations of co-active glomeruli in the olfactory bulb (OB).
evidence: This claim draws from established knowledge about olfactory encoding.

claim: A synthetic or configural representation of the odor object is first formed in piriform cortex.
source: This elemental odor code is then integrated in the piriform cortex (PCx) where a synthetic or configural representation of the odor object is first formed (Gottfried, 2010; Wilson and Sullivan, 2011; Howard and Gottfried, 2014) but see Barwich, 2019.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on olfactory processing.

claim: Projections from OB to PCx are diffuse and overlapping.
source: Projections from OB to PCx are diffuse and overlapping (Sosulski et al., 2011; Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011) allowing individual principal neurons in PCx to integrate inputs from different and possibly random subsets of glomeruli.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Individual principal neurons in PCx integrate inputs from different and possibly random subsets of glomeruli.
source: Projections from OB to PCx are diffuse and overlapping (Sosulski et al., 2011; Ghosh et al., 2011; Miyamichi et al., 2011) allowing individual principal neurons in PCx to integrate inputs from different and possibly random subsets of glomeruli.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the diffuse projection pattern and citations.

claim: Diffuse projections from OB to PCx activate odor-specific ensembles of neurons distributed across PCx.
source: The diffuse projections from OB to PCx activate odor-specific ensembles of neurons distributed across PCx [Stettler and Axel, 2009; Roland et al., 2017] whose concerted activity encodes odor identity (Miura et al., 2012; Bolding and Franks, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PCx ensemble activity.

claim: Concerted activity of PCx ensembles encodes odor identity.
source: The diffuse projections from OB to PCx activate odor-specific ensembles of neurons distributed across PCx [Stettler and Axel, 2009; Roland et al., 2017] whose concerted activity encodes odor identity (Miura et al., 2012; Bolding and Franks, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on odor encoding.

claim: Principal cells in PCx make excitatory synaptic connections onto other PCx cells with sparse but uniform connection probabilities.
source: However, principal cells make excitatory synaptic connections onto other PCx cells with sparse but uniform connection probabilities across millimeters of PCx, forming an extensive recurrent network, similar in synaptic organization to hippocampal CA3 (Johnson et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2011; Hagiwara et al., 2012; Guzman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical and physiological studies.

claim: PCx recurrent network is similar in synaptic organization to hippocampal CA3.
source: However, principal cells make excitatory synaptic connections onto other PCx cells with sparse but uniform connection probabilities across millimeters of PCx, forming an extensive recurrent network, similar in synaptic organization to hippocampal CA3 (Johnson et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2011; Hagiwara et al., 2012; Guzman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations comparing PCx and CA3 organization.

claim: Selective strengthening of recurrent synapses between co-responsive PCx neurons can lead to formation of cortical odor cell assemblies.
source: Selective strengthening of recurrent synapses between co-responsive PCx neurons can lead to the formation of cortical odor cell assemblies that can generate stable odor representations when OB inputs are noisy or degraded (Hasselmo et al., 1990; Ambros-Ingerson et al., 1990; Haberly, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and modeling studies.

claim: PCx populations can demonstrate pattern separation or pattern completion-like responses depending on recent training history.
source: PCx populations can demonstrate pattern separation or pattern completion-like responses depending on recent training history (Chapuis and Wilson, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Odor responses in both OB and PCx depend strongly on global brain state.
source: Odor responses in both OB and PCx are reported to depend strongly on global brain state (Murakami et al., 2005; Kato et al., 2012; Rinberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on state-dependent responses.

claim: Previous studies reported that OB responses increase under anesthesia.
source: Previous studies, using different methods, have reported that OB responses increase (Kato et al., 2012; Rinberg et al., 2006) or remain constant (Kollo et al., 2014) under anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Previous studies reported that OB responses remain constant under anesthesia.
source: Previous studies, using different methods, have reported that OB responses increase (Kato et al., 2012; Rinberg et al., 2006) or remain constant (Kollo et al., 2014) under anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OB responses reliably degraded shortly after a single injection of ketamine-xylazine anesthetic cocktail.
source: Curiously, we found that OB responses reliably degraded shortly after a single injection of a ketamine-xylazine anesthetic cocktail.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations in the current study.

claim: Intracortical synaptic connections within PCx are required for stabilization of odor representations across brain states.
source: Using a novel transgenic line and selective disruption of PCx output, we find that intracortical synaptic connections within PCx are required for this stabilization, consistent with the crucial role for recurrent connectivity in implementing cortical pattern completion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using TeLC and Ntng1-Cre mice.

claim: Anesthesia induced pronounced changes in respiration patterns in both OB and PCx.
source: Anesthesia induced pronounced changes in respiration patterns, oscillatory activity, and spontaneous spiking in both OB and PCx (Figure 1, b and c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1); see also [Murakami et al., 2005; Rinberg et al., 2006; Fontanini and Bower, 2005; Li et al., 2012].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: Anesthesia induced pronounced changes in oscillatory activity in both OB and PCx.
source: Anesthesia induced pronounced changes in respiration patterns, oscillatory activity, and spontaneous spiking in both OB and PCx (Figure 1, b and c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1); see also [Murakami et al., 2005; Rinberg et al., 2006; Fontanini and Bower, 2005; Li et al., 2012].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: Anesthesia induced pronounced changes in spontaneous spiking in both OB and PCx.
source: Anesthesia induced pronounced changes in respiration patterns, oscillatory activity, and spontaneous spiking in both OB and PCx (Figure 1, b and c; Figure 1—figure supplement 1); see also [Murakami et al., 2005; Rinberg et al., 2006; Fontanini and Bower, 2005; Li et al., 2012].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous OB firing rates in awake state were 6.58 ± 6.47 Hz (mean ± st.dev.).
source: Our measures of spontaneous OB activity (n = 187 cells; awake: (mean ± st.dev.) 6.58 ± 6.47 Hz; k/x: 2.62 ± 4.37 Hz) are similar to those observed using whole-cell recordings in vivo by Kollo et al. (n = 60 cells, awake: (mean ± st.dev.) 4.1 ± 6.7 Hz; k/x: n = 84 cells, 2.7 ± 4.6 Hz) (Kollo et al., 2014), but are substantially lower than those made with single extracellular electrodes by Rinberg et al. (n = 11 cells; awake: (mean ± st.dev.) 27.4 ± 9.7 Hz; k/x: 9.3 ± 4.4 Hz) (Rinberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements in the current study.

claim: Spontaneous OB firing rates under k/x anesthesia were 2.62 ± 4.37 Hz (mean ± st.dev.).
source: Our measures of spontaneous OB activity (n = 187 cells; awake: (mean ± st.dev.) 6.58 ± 6.47 Hz; k/x: 2.62 ± 4.37 Hz) are similar to those observed using whole-cell recordings in vivo by Kollo et al. (n = 60 cells, awake: (mean ± st.dev.) 4.1 ± 6.7 Hz; k/x: n = 84 cells, 2.7 ± 4.6 Hz) (Kollo et al., 2014), but are substantially lower than those made with single extracellular electrodes by Rinberg et al. (n = 11 cells; awake: (mean ± st.dev.) 27.4 ± 9.7 Hz; k/x: 9.3 ± 4.4 Hz) (Rinberg et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements in the current study.

claim: Differences in firing rate measurements likely stem from improved identification of lower firing-rate units using multi-site extracellular electrodes.
source: These differences likely stem from improved identification of lower firing-rate units using multi-site extracellular electrodes, longer-duration recordings, and improved spike-sorting algorithms.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about methodological differences.

claim: OB neurons were less responsive under anesthesia with fewer significantly activated or suppressed neurons.
source: OB neurons were less responsive under anesthesia, with many fewer significantly activated or suppressed neurons, and increased lifetime and population sparseness (Figure 1, f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: OB neurons showed increased lifetime and population sparseness under anesthesia.
source: OB neurons were less responsive under anesthesia, with many fewer significantly activated or suppressed neurons, and increased lifetime and population sparseness (Figure 1, f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PCx responsivity shifted only subtly under anesthesia and toward greater activation.
source: Yet, despite reduced input from OB, PCx responsivity shifted only subtly and, in fact, toward greater activation (Figure 1, h and i; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), due largely to an increase in signal-to-noise ratio as spontaneous activity levels in PCx dropped under anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The shift toward greater PCx activation under anesthesia was due largely to an increase in signal-to-noise ratio as spontaneous activity levels dropped.
source: Yet, despite reduced input from OB, PCx responsivity shifted only subtly and, in fact, toward greater activation (Figure 1, h and i; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), due largely to an increase in signal-to-noise ratio as spontaneous activity levels in PCx dropped under anesthesia.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observed data patterns.

claim: Individual cell-odor pair responses rarely switched from significantly activated to suppressed or vice versa.
source: Individual cell-odor pair responses rarely switched from significantly activated to suppressed or vice versa (OB: act. to supp.: 0.98% of activated responses.; supp. to act.: 3.7% of suppressed responses; PCx: act. to supp.: 0.81%; supp. to act: 5.0%).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of response switching.

claim: There was only a modest, positive average correlation between individual neuron tuning curves for awake and anesthetized responses in OB (0.13 ± 0.47).
source: Tuning curves for neurons in either region did not exhibit an overall tendency toward either maintained ordering or reconfiguration such that there was only a modest, positive average correlation between individual neuron tuning curves for awake and anesthetized responses (OB: 0.13 ± 0.47; PCx: 0.16 ± 0.48).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tuning curve correlations.

claim: There was only a modest, positive average correlation between individual neuron tuning curves for awake and anesthetized responses in PCx (0.16 ± 0.48).
source: Tuning curves for neurons in either region did not exhibit an overall tendency toward either maintained ordering or reconfiguration such that there was only a modest, positive average correlation between individual neuron tuning curves for awake and anesthetized responses (OB: 0.13 ± 0.47; PCx: 0.16 ± 0.48).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of tuning curve correlations.

claim: The loss of OB responsivity was largely due to decreased odor-evoked spiking under k/x anesthesia.
source: In our experiments, the loss of OB responsivity was largely due to decreased odor-evoked spiking under k/x anesthesia, rather than an increase in response variability or increased baseline firing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: PCx responsivity was preserved even though OB responsivity was consistently suppressed.
source: Crucially, however, we found that PCx responsivity was preserved even though OB responsivity was consistently suppressed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing OB and PCx responses.

claim: Responses in both OB and PCx became more correlated under anesthesia.
source: Responses in both regions became more correlated under anesthesia (Figure 1j-l).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The difference between within- versus across-odor response correlations decreased significantly more in OB than PCx under anesthesia.
source: However, even as all responses became more correlated, the difference between within- versus across-odor response correlations decreased significantly more in OB than PCx (Figure 1m; Figure 1—figure supplement 5i).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in figures.

claim: Decoding accuracy was markedly worse under anesthesia in OB.
source: Decoding accuracy was markedly worse under anesthesia in OB (Figure 1n), whereas responses in PCx were decoded equally well in either state (Figure 1o).
evidence: This claim is supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Responses in PCx were decoded equally well in awake or anesthetized state.
source: Decoding accuracy was markedly worse under anesthesia in OB (Figure 1n), whereas responses in PCx were decoded equally well in either state (Figure 1o).
evidence: This claim is supported by classifier analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: PCx maintains odor responsivity when OB input is degraded.
source: These data indicate that PCx maintains odor responsivity when OB input is degraded, but not whether the cortical odor representations themselves are preserved across states.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the responsivity and decoding data.

claim: There were many more robust responses in PCx than OB (PCx: 118/237; OB: 21/102 total awake responses).
source: There were many more robust responses in PCx than OB (OB, 21/102 total awake responses; PCx, 118/237 total awake responses, Figure 2c, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: PCx population responses to the same odor were more correlated across states compared to OB.
source: Compared to OB, PCx population responses to the same odor were more correlated across states (Figure 2d) and were more separable from responses to other odors (Figure 2e), indicating again that population odor representations are better preserved across states in PCx.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: PCx population responses were more separable from responses to other odors across states compared to OB.
source: Compared to OB, PCx population responses to the same odor were more correlated across states (Figure 2d) and were more separable from responses to other odors (Figure 2e), indicating again that population odor representations are better preserved across states in PCx.
evidence: This claim is supported by separation analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cross-state decoding was better in PCx than OB.
source: Cross-state decoding was better in PCx than OB (Figure 2f), indicating that PCx could extract and selectively represent stimulus-specific information from partial and noisy OB input.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-state decoding analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: PCx could extract and selectively represent stimulus-specific information from partial and noisy OB input.
source: Cross-state decoding was better in PCx than OB (Figure 2f), indicating that PCx could extract and selectively represent stimulus-specific information from partial and noisy OB input.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cross-state decoding results.

claim: State accounted for most of the variance in responses across states in both OB and PCx using standard PCA.
source: Nevertheless, cross-state decoding using spike counts was relatively poor in both OB and PCx, and Principal Components Analysis (PCA) indicated that state accounted for most of the variance in responses across states in both regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In PCx, responses to the same odor overlapped almost completely in stimulus-specific feature space across states.
source: However, in PCx responses to the same odor overlapped almost completely , indicating that the stimulus-specific features of the cortical odor response are almost identical across states and better preserved than their inputs (Figure 2h and i).
evidence: This claim is supported by demixed PCA analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The stimulus-specific features of the cortical odor response are almost identical across states and better preserved than their inputs.
source: However, in PCx responses to the same odor overlapped almost completely , indicating that the stimulus-specific features of the cortical odor response are almost identical across states and better preserved than their inputs (Figure 2h and i).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the demixed PCA overlap analysis.

claim: PCx actively transforms degraded OB output to represent the stimulus more faithfully than the input it receives.
source: Thus, regardless of whether downstream processing is fixed or adaptive, PCx actively transforms degraded OB output to represent the stimulus more faithfully than the input it receives.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cross-state representation analyses.

claim: Robust OB responses had significantly shorter latencies than state-specific responses.
source: Instead, robust OB responses had significantly shorter latencies than state-specific responses (Figure 3f).
evidence: This claim is supported by latency analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Robust responses in PCx had shorter latencies than state-specific ones.
source: However, robust responses in PCx not only had shorter latencies (Figure 3, g-l), but were also substantially stronger than state-specific ones (Figure 3k), indicating that robust responses are actively amplified within PCx.
evidence: This claim is supported by latency analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Robust responses in PCx were substantially stronger than state-specific ones.
source: However, robust responses in PCx not only had shorter latencies (Figure 3, g-l), but were also substantially stronger than state-specific ones (Figure 3k), indicating that robust responses are actively amplified within PCx.
evidence: This claim is supported by peak firing rate analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Robust responses are actively amplified within PCx.
source: However, robust responses in PCx not only had shorter latencies (Figure 3, g-l), but were also substantially stronger than state-specific ones (Figure 3k), indicating that robust responses are actively amplified within PCx.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the strength and latency data.

claim: Piriform cortex contains two distinct classes of principal cells: pyramidal cells and semilunar cells.
source: PCx contains two distinct classes of principal cells: pyramidal cells (PYRs), which are located primarily in deeper layer II and receive both OB and recurrent collateral inputs, and semilunar cells (SLs), which are more superficial and receive strong OB input but weak or no recurrent input (Figure 4a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Choy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies and schematic in Figure 4.

claim: Pyramidal cells are located primarily in deeper layer II and receive both OB and recurrent collateral inputs.
source: PCx contains two distinct classes of principal cells: pyramidal cells (PYRs), which are located primarily in deeper layer II and receive both OB and recurrent collateral inputs, and semilunar cells (SLs), which are more superficial and receive strong OB input but weak or no recurrent input (Figure 4a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Choy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Semilunar cells are more superficial and receive strong OB input but weak or no recurrent input.
source: PCx contains two distinct classes of principal cells: pyramidal cells (PYRs), which are located primarily in deeper layer II and receive both OB and recurrent collateral inputs, and semilunar cells (SLs), which are more superficial and receive strong OB input but weak or no recurrent input (Figure 4a; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Choy et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Ntng1-Cre mouse line selectively expresses Cre recombinase in semilunar cells in PCx.
source: To test whether recurrent connectivity predicts response stability, we generated a Netrin G1-Cre mouse line (Ntng1-Cre) that selectively expresses Cre recombinase in SLs in PCx (Figure 4, b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental validation shown in Figure 4.

claim: 22.4 ± 16.0% of recorded cells were opto-tagged, putative SL cells.
source: We then virally expressed either Cre-dependent Archaeorhodopsin-3 (Arch), Jaws, or Channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) in PCx to optogenetically differentiate SLs from PYRs during population recordings (Figure 4, d-f, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; 22.4 ± 16.0% opto-tagged, putative SL cells, n = 12 recordings).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic tagging.

claim: Odor responses were better-preserved across states in PYRs than SLs.
source: Indeed, odor responses were better-preserved across states in PYRs than SLs: (Figure 4, g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing PYR and SL responses shown in Figure 4.

claim: SLs recapitulated the degradation of OB representations under anesthesia.
source: SLs also recapitulated the degradation of OB representations under anesthesia (Figure 4, i and j) and the poor cross-state decoding (Figure 4k), whereas PYRs successfully recovered representations across states.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: PYRs successfully recovered representations across states.
source: SLs also recapitulated the degradation of OB representations under anesthesia (Figure 4, i and j) and the poor cross-state decoding (Figure 4k), whereas PYRs successfully recovered representations across states.
evidence: This claim is supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Two PCx cell populations receiving the same feedforward input but distinguished by their recurrent connectivity differentially recover odor representations when OB input is degraded.
source: Thus, two PCx cell populations, receiving the same feedforward input but distinguished by their recurrent connectivity, differentially recover odor representations when OB input is degraded.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the PYR vs SL comparison.

claim: Odors could be accurately identified using PCx activity at least 4 s after odor offset in control PCx.
source: In control PCx, odors could be accurately identified using activity at least 4 s after odor offset, but odor information decayed much more rapidly after odor offset in TeLC-infected PCx (Figure 7, a-c).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-time decoding analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Odor information decayed much more rapidly after odor offset in TeLC-infected PCx.
source: In control PCx, odors could be accurately identified using activity at least 4 s after odor offset, but odor information decayed much more rapidly after odor offset in TeLC-infected PCx (Figure 7, a-c).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-time decoding analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Odor-evoked activation patterns in SLs were less stable than those in simultaneously recorded PYRs.
source: Similarly, odor-evoked activation patterns in SLs were less stable than those in simultaneously recorded PYRs in Ntng1-Cre mice (Figure 7, e-h).
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-time decoding analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: OB representations decayed only slightly more rapidly than in PCx.
source: However, we note that OB representations decayed only slightly more rapidly than in PCx (Figure 7, i-l), leaving open the possibility that OB-PCx interactions contribute to short-term maintenance of odor representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-time decoding analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: PCx activity exhibits features consistent with attractor network function including preserved sensory representations when upstream representations are degraded.
source: PCx activity exhibits several features that are consistent with attractor network function. First, cortical sensory representations are preserved even when upstream representations are substantially degraded.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cross-state preservation data.

claim: Odor responses stabilize over multiple presentations, reflecting formation of cortical odor templates.
source: Second, odor responses stabilize over multiple presentations, reflecting, in part, the formation of cortical odor templates.
evidence: This claim is supported by trial-by-trial stabilization analysis.

claim: Odor representations persist after the stimulus has ended.
source: Third, odor representations persist after the stimulus has ended.
evidence: This claim is supported by cross-time decoding analysis.

claim: Responses destabilize and do not converge in a trial-number dependent manner after blocking transmitter release from PCx principal neurons.
source: First, responses destabilize and do not converge in a trial-number dependent manner after blocking transmitter release from PCx principal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by TeLC experiments showing loss of trial-dependent stabilization.

claim: Odor responses are more stable in recurrently connected PYRs than in SLs.
source: Second, odor responses are more stable in recurrently connected PYRs than in SLs.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of PYR and SL responses.

claim: Recurrent connections within PCx are capable of undergoing plasticity and forming self-reinforcing neural ensembles.
source: Recurrent connections within PCx are capable of undergoing plasticity and forming self-reinforcing neural ensembles (Kanter and Haberly, 1990; Jung et al., 1990; Poo and Isaacson, 2007), which endows the circuit with the ability to form coherent sensory representations from noisy input (Wilson and Sullivan, 2011; Haberly, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PCx plasticity.

claim: PCx circuits can form coherent sensory representations from noisy input.
source: Recurrent connections within PCx are capable of undergoing plasticity and forming self-reinforcing neural ensembles (Kanter and Haberly, 1990; Jung et al., 1990; Poo and Isaacson, 2007), which endows the circuit with the ability to form coherent sensory representations from noisy input (Wilson and Sullivan, 2011; Haberly, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Long-range recurrent circuits recruit strong, global feedback inhibition, implementing a 'temporal winner-take-all' filter.
source: Previously, we described how long-range recurrent circuits recruit strong, global feedback inhibition, implementing a 'temporal winner-take-all' filter that allows the earliest-active OB inputs to largely define the PCx response and thereby make PCx odor responses robust to changes in odorant concentration (Bolding and Franks, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Recurrent connections help selectively recruit specific subsets of similarly responsive PCx principal cells.
source: This net-inhibitory process is complementary to the more constructive role for recurrent circuits that we propose here, in which recurrent connections help selectively recruit specific subsets of similarly responsive PCx principal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current experimental results.

claim: Trial-dependent stabilization of PCx odor representations emerges through a Hebbian learning process at recurrent synapses between co-active PCx principal cells.
source: We have described a trial-dependent stabilization of PCx odor representations, which we propose emerges through a Hebbian learning process at recurrent synapses between co-active PCx principal cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the trial-dependent stabilization data and theoretical considerations.

claim: Cholinergic, noradrinergic, and GABAergic modulators selectively affect recurrent but not afferent synapses in PCx.
source: Intriguingly, cholinergic (Hasselmo and Bower, 1992), noradrinergic (Hasselmo et al., 1997), and GABAergic (Tang and Hasselmo, 1994; Franks and Isaacson, 2005) modulators selectively affect recurrent but not afferent synapses in PCx, providing a mechanism to coherently and flexibly implement task-dependent computations in the same circuit.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on neuromodulation.
